a.headline: Meet Krea 3: the fast, easy-to-use tool built for editing (not replacing) your work
a.summary: Krea 3 positions itself as an AI editing tool that enhances your existing creative work rather than generating from scratch, which is a meaningful distinction worth examining. As AI tools flood the market, understanding which ones genuinely support designer authorship versus which ones displace it is essential knowledge for working practitioners.

a.headline: The Kiwibank sheep went viral for all the wrong reasons, and there is something every brand can learn from it
a.summary: The Kiwibank AI mascot controversy shows how generative tools can undermine brand control when outputs circulate beyond the intended context. For design students working on brand identity, this is a sharp reminder that AI-generated assets carry unpredictable reputational risk.

a.headline: Kylie Minogue songs already used to train AI as tech firms strong-arm Australian government, music body warns
a.summary: Music industry bodies are warning that AI companies are lobbying governments to weaken copyright protections, with Australia potentially the only country considering such changes. This has direct implications for designers and illustrators whose visual work faces the same extraction without consent.

a.headline: This weird legal case could change how we think of copyright forever
a.summary: A copyright case currently working through the courts could fundamentally redefine what counts as authorship and ownership in an era of AI-generated imagery. Design students should follow this closely as the outcome will shape the legal landscape of creative practice for years to come.

b.headline: Microsoft pulls out of AI datacentre project in Essex over power supply concerns
b.summary: Microsoft has withdrawn from a major UK AI data centre project because the local power grid cannot meet its energy demands, exposing the enormous electricity appetite behind the AI tools designers use daily. This is a concrete illustration of how AI infrastructure competes directly with wider energy systems.

b.headline: Data Centers Have a New PR Plan: Your Kid Field Trip
b.summary: Data centre operators are running school outreach programmes to counter growing public backlash about their land, water, and energy use. Recognising how industries manage the optics of environmental harm is useful critical thinking for designers working in sustainability communication.

b.headline: Is coal really making a comeback?
b.summary: Demand for coal is rising again in part because AI data centres are consuming electricity faster than renewable sources can supply it. This piece connects the computational scale of AI directly to fossil fuel dependency, a link that every designer choosing to use generative tools should understand.

c.headline: SourceType Dictionary of the Illegible explores what happens when typography stops making sense
c.summary: Laurenz Brunner examines typeforms that resist readability, from metal band logos to censorship-evading coded scripts, raising sharp questions about legibility, control, and the limits of algorithmic text processing. For visual communication students, this is a critical project about what typography can do that machine learning struggles to parse.

c.headline: Andre Britz draws dimly remembered landscapes, in a book held together with a pink elastic band
c.summary: German graphic designer Andre Britz creates deliberately unfinished drawings of half-remembered places, bound in a lo-fi physical format that resists the polish and resolution of digital production. The project is a quiet argument for memory, imperfection, and the handmade as meaningful creative positions.

c.headline: Wildwood: The Exhibition reveals how Laika builds stop-motion worlds
c.summary: The Laika exhibition at the Design Museum puts handcrafted miniature sets and hand-animated puppets centre stage, making a powerful case for physical fabrication as a distinct and irreplaceable creative discipline. At a moment when AI video generation promises effortless world-building, this exhibition asks what is lost when the hand leaves the process entirely.
